112 REPORT OF UNITED STATES CIVIL SERVICE COMMISSION. 
January 27, 1910. 
Mrs. Nannie M. Wayland may be reinstated in the clerical grade in any department without regard to the length of time that she has been separated from the service. This Executive order supersedes an Executive order issued on April 7, 1909, which permitted Mrs. Wayland’s reinstatement in the classified service of the Treasury Department. Mrs. Wayland has been temporarily employed on different occasions ager the War Department in the Philippine Islands and also in the Philippine classi- fied service. 
January 27, 1910. 
Upon the recommendation of the Postmaster General, with the concurrence of the Civil Service Commission, John N. Parsons may be reinstated as a letter carrier in the postal service with a view to his promotion to the position of post-office inspector, the one-year limitation of the reinstatement rule being waived because of his excellent record as carrier and his efficient service as postmaster at Yonkers, N. Y. 
January 31, 1910. 
Mr. J. F. Boepple may be appointed to the position of shell expert at $1,200 per annum in the Biological Station, Fairport, Iowa, Bureau of Fisheries, Department of Commerce and Labor, without examination under the civil-service rules. The Fairport Biological Station is devoted primarily to investigation and experi- mentation regarding the culture of fresh-water mussels and their artificial propagation in the interest of the pearl-button industry. Mr. Boepple is said to have been the first man in America to use the shells of the fresh-water mussels in the manufacture of pearl buttons and to demonstrate that excellent buttons can be made from these shells. The demonstration of this fact has resulted in the building up of an industry the output of which is valued at $6,000,000. Mr. Boepple has had large experience in buying shells and in the manufacture of buttons and also in observing the mussels on the natural beds in many different streams. Within the last three years he has 
been employed at various times by the Bureau of Fisheries as a temporary assistant at the Ohio River and Cannelton, Ind., stations in connection with the pearl- mussel industry of the bureau and proved himself very efficient. The position of shell expert is in the competitive classified service, and in view of Mr. Boepple’s demonstrated qualification for the duties of the position and the fact that there would probably be no competition in an examination if held, the Civil 
Service Commission recommended his appointment by Executive order in view of the facts presented by the department as above briefly set forth. 
February 4, 1910. 
John H. Dickinson, formerly employed as an inspector in the Quartermaster’s Department of the Army, who was dismissed more than one year ago on account of alleged irregularities which were afterwards found to be groundless, may be reinstated as an inspector without regard to the provision of the civil-service rules limiting rein￾statement to one year after separation. This order was recommended by the Secretary of War and the Civil Service Com- mission. 
February 15, 1910. 
John G. Curran, long employed in the public building at Cleveland, Ohio, as assistant custodian-janitor, may be reappointed in the Assistant Custodian and Janitor Service under the designation of assistant custodian, United States Post-Office, Cus- tom-House, and Court-House Building at Cleveland, Ohio, notwithstanding he has been more than one year separated from the service because of the abandonment of the old building. : 
This order is issued because of Mr. Curran’s long and satisfactory service in a similar position and because in a short time the new public building at Cleveland, Ohio, will be ready for occupancy, and the department desires to avail itself of Mr. Curran’s experience and known fitness as assistant custodian of that building. 
March 7, 1910. 
Henry Bartalot, formerly employed as a marine engineer in the Quartermaster’s Department at Large, may be reinstated as a marine engineer without regard to the length of separation from the service. This action is taken on recommendation of the Secretary of War and the Civil 
Service Commission, based on a report of the Quartermaster General indicating that Mr. Bartalot’s discharge from the position of marine engineer on March 17, 1906, was not justified and as the commission, if the case had been presented within one year 
from Bartalot’s discharge, would have permitted his reinstatement under the rules.

REPORT OF UNITED STATES CIVIL SERVICE COMMISSION. 113 
March 15, 1910. 
James A. Compton, William E. Dulin, and George P. Meyer may be reinstated in the Pension Office without regard to the fact that they have been separated from the service for more than one year. This action is based upon the statement of the Secre- tary of the Interior that under similar circumstances separations from the service would not in general be imposed for a similar offense and that the men suffered an injustice in their removal. Their reinstatement is favored by the Civil Service Com- mission. 
April 18, 1910. 
Mr. Collinson Lewis Warwick may be appointed nautical expert in the Coast and Geodetic Survey without examination under the civil-service rules, it appearing that his services are essential in the prosecution of the work of the Coast Pilot Division. This order is made upon the concurrent recommendation of the Secretary of Com- merce and Labor and the Civil Service Commission, based upon Mr. Warwick’s long experience at sea, his large acquaintance with the masters, mates, and local pilots of the country, upon whose good will and confidence the obtaining of much valuable information depends, and his former satisfactory service asa mate in the Coast and Geo- detic Survey, all of which tend to show his qualifications for the position. May 11, 1910. 
Miss Helen M. Bullis may be appointed special inspectress in the Immigration Service, Department of Commerce and Labor, without examination under the civil- service rules. 
This action is authorized on the recommendation of the Secretary of Commerce and Labor because of Miss Bullis’s ascertained fitness for conducting investigations necessary in connection with the new statute concerning white slavery (amendment of immigration act, approved Mar. 26, 1910) and with the concurrence of the Civil Service Commission. Miss Bullis has been employed since September 1, 1907, either temporarily or in a position not subject to examination, upon similar work. 
May 12, 1910. 
Henry Suberkrup may be appointed to the position of guard to act as musical instructor to the prisoners at the United States Penitentiary, Leavenworth, Kans. without examination under the civil-service rules, in view of the Attorney General's report of the desirability of undertaking the musical instruction of prisoners at that institution and of Mr. Suberkrup’s availability and fitness for the position, the Civil Service Commission concurring. 
June 22, 1910.

REPORT OF UNITED STATES CIVIL SERVICE COMMISSION. 139 
The opinion of the President conveyed in the letter of his Secretary will be treated as an Executive order. (Minute 1, Mar. 23, 1912.) 
PETITIONS TO CONGRESS BY CIVIL-SERVICE EMPLOYEES, 
April 8, 1912.1 
It is hereby ordered that petitions or other communications regarding public busi- ness addressed to Congress or either House or any committee or Member thereof by officers or employees in the civil service of the United States shall be transmitted through the heads of their respective departments or offices, who shall forward them without delay with such comment as they may deem requisite in the public interest. Officers and employees are strictly prohibited either directly or indirectly from at- tempting to secure legislation, or to influence pending legislation, except in the manner above prescribed. This order supersedes the Executive orders of January 31, 1902, January 25, 1906, and November 26, 1909, regarding the same general matter 
EXCEPTIONS IN MACHINE SHOP OF THE BUREAU OF THE CENSUS. 
August 21, 1812. - 
With a view to meeting emergencies in the machine shop of the Bureau of the Census, in connection with the continuation of the Thirteenth Decennial Census work during the fiscal year 1913, the Secretary of Commerce and Labor is hereby authorized to employ, until June 30, 1913, without reference to the civil-service rules, such machinists, toolmakers, electricians, and apprentice boys (machinists) as may be necessary for the prosecution of the work whenever, in his opinion, it is not prac- ticable to make such appointments from the civil-service lists. This order extends the authority for similar appointments contained in the Executive order of December 29, 1909. The Civil Service Commission concurs with the department in recommending this order, in view of the representations of the department as to its necessity. ! 
EMPLOYMENT IN PENSION OFFICE OF FORMER TREASURY EMPLOYEES. 
August 24, 1912. 
The Commissioner of Pensions is directed to employ as extra clerks under the appro- priation of $300,000 carried in the sundry civil act approved August 24, 1912, the 30 persons heretofore employed in the office of the Auditor for the Post Office Depart- ment whose names are on the list furnished to the President in a letter of the Secre- tary of the Treasury dated August 22, 1912, said appropriation act authorizing the Commissioner of Pensions to employ clerks heretofore employed in other departments of the Government service. All of these persons except one have a competitive classified status and will be eligible for reinstatement in the Treasury Department under the civil-service rules. 
MODERATOR OF A TOWN MEETING MAY BE A CLASSIFIED EMPLOYEE, 
August 24, 1912. 
The temporary office of moderator of a town meeting and offices of a like character are hereby excepted from the operation of the Executive order of January 17, 1873, prohibiting persons in the Federal civil service from holding office under the charter or ordinances of any municipal corporation, and may be held by persons in the execu- tive civil service. Membership in the civil service ought not to prevent an employee from taking part in the ordinary municipal affairs of the community in which he lives, where that part does not involve permanent service but only such a temporary duty as that of acting as chairman of a municipal business meeting, where such service is not compensated by any salary or other emolument, and where the attention required by such service does not interfere with the regular and efficient discharge of the duties of the Federal office held. In the exercise of the privilege granted by this order officers and employees must not neglect their official duties and must not engage in national, State, or county political activity in violation of the civil-service rules; and in seeking the local offices named or in performing the duties thereof employees shall not use the authority or influence of their Federal positions nor take an active part in political management or 
 
in political campaigns. 
1 See section 6, Public Act No. 336, approved Aug. 24, 1912, p. 73.

August 24, 1912. 
The position of special employee in the Internal-Revenue Service shall hereafter be regarded as classified under the civil-service act and rules. No such special employee now serving shall be regarded as classified hereunder or shall acquire any right of promotion or transfer under the rules unless he is specially commended therefor by the Commissioner of Internal Revenue, with the approval of the Secretary of the Treasury, because of efficient services rendered, and whose name is embraced in the is furnished to the Civil Service Commission by the Treasury Department of this 
ate. The Treasury Department may make appointments of special employees for a period not exceeding 30 days or not exceeding 45 days in any one quarter of any fiscal year without reference to the civil-service rules. This order shall take effect October 1, 1912, and is issued with the concurrence of the Secretary of the Treasury and the Civil Service Commission. 
CLASSIFICATION AUTHORIZED OF CERTAIN EXPERTS IN THE DEPARTMENT OF AGRI- CULTURE. August 26, 1912. 
Not exceeding 115 persons appointed as experts and agents without examination under Subdivision IX, section 1 of Schedule A, of the civil-service rules, and who now are engaged upon work similar to that of competitive employees, and who are especially recommended by the Secretary of Agriculture because of their proved capacity for efficient service may be transferred to appropriate competitive positions in the Department of Agriculture. By Executive order of this date the provision of the civil-service rules permitting the appointment of agents and experts of the Department of Agriculture without examination is amended to fix more definitely the conditions under which appoint- ments can be made. ORDERS EXCEPTING PERSONS NAMED FROM THE REQUIREMENTS OF 
THE RULES. 
July 7, 1911. 
Henry M. Camp was appointed on August 1, 1895, in the Norwalk, Conn., post office, in the classified civil service, and was transferred on February 8, 1901, to the office of the First Assistant Postmaster General upon the clerk examination. He resigned from the position of clerk at $1,400 per annum on September 1, 1908. His resignation was voluntary, and his record as a clerk was satisfactory. The Civil Service Commission certifies that Mr. Camp’s reinstatement may be justified on the ground of capability and efficiency, but that as he has been separated from the service for more than a year, and as he resigned in order that he might occupy his time in politics, it declines to recommend his reinstatement, following in this regard a precedent which had been set by a previous administration. I do not agree with the precedent. I do not mean to say that the circumstances under which one 
leaves a department, and the purpose for which it is done, might not affect the right to reinstatement, but I do not think that it ought to be adopted as an iron rule that leaving the service in order to engage in some political activity necessarily bars a return to the service. For this reason, Mr. Camp will be reinstated in the classified service without regard to the length of time he has been separated therefrom. 
July 14, 1911. 
Mr. Charles L. Dooley, formerly an immigrant inspector in the Immigration Service, who served faithfully for more than three years, may be reinstated without regard to the fact that he has been separated from the service for more than a year. In view of the statement of the Secretary of Commerce and Labor that the service would be benefited by Mr. Dooley’s reinstatement, and that the department could have no better proof of fitness than the record which Mr. Dooley made in the service, the Civil Service Commission joins with the department in the recommendation of this order.

REPORT OF UNITED STATES CIVIL SERVICE COMMISSION. 141 
July 31, 1911. 
Mr. Thomas Richardson, who has been serving as postmaster at Port Gibson, Miss., since July 12, 1898, may be appointed to an appropriate position in the competitive classified service at Washington where his postal experience will be available, without reference to the requirement of examination under the civil service rules. Investigation and report made to the satisfaction of the President shows the fitness of Mr. Richardson, after 15 years’ service in the Post Office Department, for the appointment at Washington in the competitive classified service. The commission recommends the issuance of the order. 
August 2, 1911. 
The provisions of the Executive order of January 17, 1873, prohibiting Federal employees from holding office under any State, Territorial, or municipal government are hereby waived to permit Sylvester P. Bartlett, a field superintendent in the Bureau of Fisheries, to hold the position of secretary to the Illinois State Fish Com- mission, in view of the mutual advantages thereby secured to the State commission and the Bureau of Fisheries. This order is recommended by the Civil Service Com- mission. 
August 2, 1911. 
Charles B. Bateman may be transferred from the navy-yard service to any classified mechanical position in the departments at Washington for which his experience of 14 years as a machinist qualifies him. This order, which 1s concurred in by the Civil Service Commission, is issued in view of an unfortunate situation in which Mr. Bateman is shown to have been placed, and the fact being recognized that the good of the service is advanced by increasing the comfort and peacefulness, and hence the efficiency, of its working force. This matter is fully set forth in the commission’s letter of August 1, 1911. 
August 9, 1911. 
An appointment may be made to the position of secretary of the Interstate Com- merce Commission to succeed Mr. E. A. Moseley, who occupied this position from the date of its classification until his death, which recently occurred. The Inter- state Commerce Commission deems it desirable to appoint one who is not within the classified service, although in the employment of the commission. The Civil Service Commission joins in recommending this order.

In view of the facts the Secretary of Commerce and Labor recommends the appoint￾ment of Mrs. Hampton. 
The Civil Service Commission does not concur in the recommendation for an 
Executive order. 
June 11, 1912. 
Mrs. May Stanley may be appointed to a position in the classified service without examination under the civil-service rules. Mrs. Stanley is the widow of Will H. Stanley, superintendent of the Soboba Indian School, California, who was murdered May 3, 1912, by an Indian under the juris- diction of that superintendency. Mr. Stanley left two dependent children. Mrs. Stanley has been employed for several years in excepted positions in the Indian Service. She attended Dickinson County High School, Kansas, the Lebanon Val- ley College, Pennsylvania, and the University of Kansas, and the department believes that she will render efficient service in the capacity of teacher. In view of the facts the Civil Service Commission joins with the department in recommending the issuance of an Executive order. 
June 15, 1912. 
Mr. Oscar Wenderoth may be reinstated in the classified service to the position of Supervising Architect without regard to the length of time that he has been sepa- rated from the service. 
Mr. Wenderoth served as senior architectural draftsman and foreman of construction - in and under the Office of the Supervising Architect, from March 8, 1897, when he was appointed through appropriate examination, to April 16, 1900, when he resigned; and again from March 10, 1903, when he was reinstated by Executive order as senior architectural draftsman, to July 31, 1904. 
In view of his previous service, his experience, and his proved efficiency, the commission joins with the Secretary of the Treasury in recommending this order. 
June 19, 1912. 
Mr. M. M. Dodge may be transferred, before the completion of his probationary 
period, from the position of clerk in the War Department to naturalization examiner at Pittsburgh, Pa. : 
The transfer of Mr. Dodge was desired by the department because of his high edu- cational attainments, mature judgment, and experience in law and in administrative matters. Mr. Dodge is regarded by the Division of Naturalization as peculiarly fitted for the duties of the position at Pittsburgh to which he is to be transferred. Under the civil-service rules an employee is not eligible for transfer from one depart- ment to another until he has served for six months and has received absolute appoint￾ment, and the Civil Service Commission was unable to concur with the department in the recommendation for an Executive order. 
June 19, 1912. 
Mr. John G. Lerch may be Spoil without examination as private secretary to Mr. lugene G. Hay, member of the Board of General Appraisers. The position is one of a highly confidential nature, as the secretary to the general appraiser must of necessity know in many instances in advance of the promulgation of decisions what the decisions will be. 
Mr. Lerch has had considerable previous experience in the capacity of secretary and has passed the civil-service examination in stenography and typewriting. The Civil Service Commission does not concur in the recommendation for an Executive order. 
July 10, 1912. 
Mr. Leroy A. McGee may be reinstated to the position of post-office inspector without reference to the time limit upon eligibility for reinstatement. 
Mr. McGee served for four years as a teacher in the Indian Service, for three years as a clerk in the Office of the Auditor for the Post Office Department, and three years as a post-office inspector, resigning from the latter position on October 7, 1910. He has passed the teacher examination, the post-office inspector examination, and the immigrant inspector examination with good ratings. The chief post-office inspector reports that he was a good inspector, that his work was satisfactory, that there is nothing in the files which would be considered against his reinstatement, and that since his resignation Mr. McGee has been practicing law. In view of his good record and the fact that his experience since leaving the service has been such as to increase his efficiency, the Civil Service Commission joins with the Postmaster General in recom- mending the reinstatement,

July 12, 1912. 
The following-named employees of the Tariff Board who have been especially recom- mended for retention in the public service may be transferred or appointed to appro- riate positions in the competitive classified service with the approval of the Civil A, Commission; but in the case of any such person who has not a competitive status or who has not passed an appropriate examination for the position to which 
appointment is proposed the Civil Service Commission may apply such tests of fitness as 1t deems necessary before approval: Mr. Leo Rullmann, Mrs. B. C. Woodford, Mr. Herve W. Kitzmiller, Mrs. Rose R. Aydelotte, Miss Anna E. Hutchinson, Mrs. Max West, Mr. N. I. Stone, Miss Mary E. Bishop, Mr. A. L. Colton, Mr. J. L. F. Ingold, Mr. James Otey, Mr. Wilson Evans, Mr. Travers Pinn, Mr. J. Garfield Harris. Eligibility under this order shall cease at the expiration of one year from the date of the person’s separation from the Tariff Board. This order is issued upon the recommendation of the chairman of the Tariff Board, with the approval of the Civil Service Commission, on account of the faithful and meritorious service of the employees, most of whom have had considerable experience in the Government service, although not in all cases in the classified service, but in - no case less than 18 months. 
July 19, 1912. 
Mr. Dorsey E. Phillips, of Missouri, may be appointed to a clerical position in the competitive classified service without reference to the civil-service rules. Mr. Phillips served for five years in the Regular Army prior to May 30, 1898. He passed the clerk examination held at St. Joseph, Mo., on March 22, 1909, with a rating of 78.35 and was temporarily employed as a result of this examination from October 25, 1909, to Feb- ruary 18, 1910. He also passed the census-clerk examination with a rating of 80.25, as a result of which he received appointment in the Bureau of the Census and served from September 6, 1910, to February 29, 1912, when he was separated on account of a necessary reduction of force. The Civil Service Commission does not recommend the approval of this order. 
July 23, 1912. 
Mr. Isaac D. Laferty may be reinstated in the Bureau of Pensions, Department of the Interior, without reference to the time limit of eligibility for reinstatement under the civil-service rules. Mr. Laferty was appointed to a clerical position in the Pension Office on August 11,

Mr. Louis H. Eberlein may be reinstated to an appropriate classified position in the (Customs Service at New York without regard to the length of time he has been sepa- rated from the service. Mr. Eberlein was separated from the service on May 26, 1910, on a charge of accepting money from importers and underweighing dutiable merchan- dise. Upon a rehearing of the case by the surveyor of customs at New York the opinion was reached that neither the charges as a whole nor any specification had been sustained, and in view of Mr. Eberlein’s previous good record recommendation was made that the charges be dismissed. The Attorney General, after review of the case, stated that he deemed it a case where an honest man suffered from the general atmosphere of his surroundings, and that the recommendation of the surveyor of customs should be acted upon and Mr. Eberlein reinstated. Mr. Taylor was appointed deputy collector of internal revenue at $1,600, in the second district, New York, on May 1, 1900, on the war revenue roll, and resigned October 31, 1902. The officials of the Treasury Department report that Mr. Taylor made a highly efficient officer and in point of intelligence, education, and address is above the average internal-revenue officer, and that he would be a valuable acqui￾gition to the force. January 8, 1913. 
Mr. William B. Kilpatrick may be restored to the competitive service without regard to the year limitation upon reinstatement. 
Mr. Kilpatrick entered the Navy Department as a clerk, through competitive examination, in 1902 and was rapidly promoted to $1,800. In 1907 he resigned, and reentered the service August 24, 1912, as private secretary to the Assistant Secretary of the Treasury. The Treasury Department states that his selection for private sec- retary was made because of the character of his work in the Navy Department, and that his work in the Treasury Department has been excellent. By his death Mrs. Croghan became the sole sup- port of her young son and an aunt.
